claim: 18 epilepsy patients participated in the study listening to natural, continuous speech or music.
source: Using whole-brain intracranial EEG recordings in 18 epilepsy patients listening to natural, continuous speech or music, we investigated the presence of frequency-specific and network-level brain activity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of patients and the experimental conditions.

claim: The majority of focal and network-level neural activity is shared between speech and music processing.
source: We show that the majority of focal and network-level neural activity is shared between speech and music processing.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figures 2, 3, and 8.

claim: There is an absence of anatomical regional selectivity for speech and music processing.
source: Our data also reveal an absence of anatomical regional selectivity.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by population prevalence analyses shown in Figures 5, 6, and 10.

claim: Domain-selective neural responses are restricted to distributed and frequency-specific coherent oscillations.
source: Instead, domain-selective neural responses are restricted to distributed and frequency-specific coherent oscillations, typical of spectral fingerprints.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by spectral and connectivity analyses.

claim: Neuroimaging studies report mixed evidence of selectivity and resource sharing between language and music processing.
source: Neuroimaging studies report mixed evidence of selectivity and resource sharing.
evidence: This statement summarizes existing literature and is supported by multiple citations in the following sentences.

claim: Some studies claim a clear distinction between brain regions exclusively dedicated to language versus other cognitive processes.
source: On one hand, one can find claims for a clear distinction between brain regions exclusively dedicated to language versus other cognitive processes (Chen et al., 2023; Fedorenko et al., 2011; Fedorenko and Blank, 2020; Friederici, 2020) and for the existence of specific and separate neural populations for speech, music, and song (Boebinger et al., 2021; Norman-Haignere et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Other neuroimaging studies suggest that brain regions supporting language and speech also support nonlinguistic functions.
source: On the other hand, other neuroimaging studies suggest that the brain regions that support language and speech also support nonlinguistic functions (Albouy et al., 2020; Fadiga et al., 2009; Koelsch, 2011; Menon et al., 2002; Robert et al., 2023; Schön et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Music training can have a positive impact on different levels of speech and language processing.
source: This point is often put forward when interpreting the positive impact music training can have on different levels of speech and language processing (Flaugnacco et al., 2015; François et al., 2013; Kraus and Chandrasekaran, 2010; Schön et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Speech unfolds faster than music.
source: However, speech unfolds faster than music (Ding et al., 2017), and while a linguistic phrase is typically shorter than a second (Inbar et al., 2020), a melodic phrase is an order of magnitude longer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A linguistic phrase is typically shorter than a second.
source: However, speech unfolds faster than music (Ding et al., 2017), and while a linguistic phrase is typically shorter than a second (Inbar et al., 2020), a melodic phrase is an order of magnitude longer.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A melodic phrase is an order of magnitude longer than a linguistic phrase.
source: However, speech unfolds faster than music (Ding et al., 2017), and while a linguistic phrase is typically shorter than a second (Inbar et al., 2020), a melodic phrase is an order of magnitude longer.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited literature on temporal characteristics of speech and music.

claim: Simple musical melodies mainly induce pitch processing in associative auditory regions.
source: These simple melodies mainly induce pitch processing in associative auditory regions (Griffiths et al., 2010) but do not recruit the entire dual-stream auditory pathways (Zatorre et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Simple melodies do not recruit the entire dual-stream auditory pathways.
source: These simple melodies mainly induce pitch processing in associative auditory regions (Griffiths et al., 2010) but do not recruit the entire dual-stream auditory pathways (Zatorre et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: High-frequency activity amplitude is a good proxy of focal neural spiking.
source: Indeed, while HFa amplitude is a good proxy of focal neural spiking (Le Van Quyen et al., 2010; Ray and Maunsell, 2011), large-scale neuronal interactions mainly rely on slower dynamics (Kayser et al., 2012; Kopell et al., 2000; Siegel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Large-scale neuronal interactions mainly rely on slower dynamics.
source: Indeed, while HFa amplitude is a good proxy of focal neural spiking (Le Van Quyen et al., 2010; Ray and Maunsell, 2011), large-scale neuronal interactions mainly rely on slower dynamics (Kayser et al., 2012; Kopell et al., 2000; Siegel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neural responses are predominantly shared between speech and music, accounting for approximately 70% of channels showing significant response compared to baseline.
source: Overall, neural responses are predominantly shared between the two domains, accounting for ~70% of the channels which showed a significant response compared to baseline (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The preferred category accounts for 3-15% of significant neural responses across frequency bands.
source: The preferred category is also systematically present, accounting for 3–15% of significant neural responses, across frequency bands.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the spectral analysis.

claim: Selective responses are more present in lower frequency bands (approximately 30% up to the alpha band).
source: Selective responses are more present in the lower frequency bands (~30% up to the alpha band), and quite marginal in the HFa band (6–12%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the spectral analysis.

claim: Selective responses are quite marginal in the high-frequency activity band (6-12%).
source: Selective responses are more present in the lower frequency bands (~30% up to the alpha band), and quite marginal in the HFa band (6–12%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the spectral analysis.

claim: High-frequency activity shared responses represent 74-86% of overall significant high-frequency activity responses.
source: For instance, HFa shared responses represent 74–86% of the overall significant HFa responses, and are visible in the left superior and middle temporal gyri, inferior parietal lobule, and the precentral, middle, and inferior frontal gyri (Figures 2F and 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data shown in Figures 2F and 3F.

claim: The left hemisphere appears to be more strongly involved in speech and music processing.
source: The left hemisphere appears to be more strongly involved, but this result is biased by the inclusion of a majority of patients with a left hemisphere exploration (Figure 1C and D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This observation is noted but attributed to sampling bias.

claim: The patterns of shared, selective, and preferred responses remain similar across hemispheres across frequency bands.
source: Also, when inspecting left and right hemispheres separately, the patterns of shared, selective, and preferred responses remain similar across hemispheres across frequency bands (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for activation and deactivation, respectively).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: For low frequencies (<15 Hz), speech selective and preferred responses were mostly deactivations and music responses were activations compared to baseline.
source: When considering separately activation (Figure 2) and deactivation (Figure 3) responses, speech and music showed complementary patterns: for low frequencies (<15 Hz) speech selective (and preferred) responses were mostly deactivations and music responses activations compared to baseline, and this pattern reversed for high frequencies (>15 Hz).
evidence: This pattern is observed in the data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The pattern of speech and music responses reversed for high frequencies (>15 Hz).
source: When considering separately activation (Figure 2) and deactivation (Figure 3) responses, speech and music showed complementary patterns: for low frequencies (<15 Hz) speech selective (and preferred) responses were mostly deactivations and music responses activations compared to baseline, and this pattern reversed for high frequencies (>15 Hz).
evidence: This pattern is observed in the data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The percentage of total channels being selective to speech or music is approximately 4 times less when considering the entire frequency spectrum compared to a single frequency band.
source: When considering the entire frequency spectrum, the percentage of total channels being selective to speech or music is ~4 times less than when considering a single frequency band.
evidence: This finding is based on cross-frequency channel selectivity analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Up to 8% of total channels are selective for speech or music in the theta band.
source: For instance, while up to 8% of the total channels are selective for speech (or music) in the theta band, this percentage always drops to ~2% when considering the cross-frequency channel selectivity.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cross-frequency selectivity analysis.

claim: The percentage of selective channels drops to approximately 2% when considering cross-frequency channel selectivity.
source: For instance, while up to 8% of the total channels are selective for speech (or music) in the theta band, this percentage always drops to ~2% when considering the cross-frequency channel selectivity.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cross-frequency selectivity analysis.

claim: The model in which low-frequency neural activity encoded the peakRates captured the most channels that significantly encoded speech and/or music acoustic features.
source: The model for which most channels significantly encoded speech and/or music acoustic features corresponded to the model in which LF neural activity encoded the peakRates (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the TRF model comparison shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Low-frequency activity encodes acoustic features in significantly more channels than high-frequency amplitude.
source: In general, the LF activity encodes the acoustic features in significantly more channels than the HFa amplitude (peakRate & LF vs. peakRate & HFa amplitude comparison: t=13.39, q<0.0001; peakRate & LF vs. envelope & HFa amplitude comparison: t=9.55, q<0.0001).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical comparisons of TRF models.

claim: The peakRates are encoded by low-frequency neural activity throughout the cortex for both speech and music.
source: Furthermore, we show that the peakRates are encoded by the LF neural activity throughout the cortex, for both speech and music (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figures 7B and C.

claim: The regions where neural activity significantly encodes the acoustic structure of stimuli extend beyond auditory regions to the temporo-parietal junction, motor cortex, inferior frontal gyrus, and anterior and central sections of the superior and middle temporal gyrus.
source: More precisely, the regions wherein neural activity significantly encodes the acoustic structure of the stimuli go well beyond auditory regions and extend to the temporo-parietal junction, motor cortex, inferior frontal gyrus, and anterior and central sections of the superior and middle temporal gyrus.
evidence: This spatial distribution is observed in the TRF analysis results.

claim: The strongest encoding values for speech are observed in the typical left-hemispheric language network, comprising the upper bank of the superior temporal gyrus, the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus, and the premotor cortex.
source: In particular, the strongest encoding values for speech are observed in the typical left-hemispheric language network, comprising the upper bank of the superior temporal gyrus, the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus, and the premotor cortex (Malik-Moraleda et al., 2022).
evidence: This finding is supported by the TRF analysis and cited literature.

claim: The best cortical tracking of the acoustic structure takes place in the auditory cortex for both speech and music.
source: Still, as expected, the best cortical tracking of the acoustic structure takes place in the auditory cortex, for both speech and music (Figure 7D).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The best encoding channels are the same for speech and music and are those located closest to or in the primary auditory cortex.
source: In other words, the best encoding channels are the same for speech and music and are those located closest to—or in—the primary auditory cortex.
evidence: This finding is based on the TRF analysis results.

claim: There was no difference in the number of significant channels between hemispheres proportionally.
source: Proportionally, we found no difference in the number of significant channels between hemispheres (i.e. speech: 41% and 44% for left and right hemispheres respectively; music: 22% and 24% for left and right hemispheres, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the TRF analysis.

claim: The peakRate & LF model yields similar TRF shape for both speech and music.
source: Finally, the peakRate & LF model, i.e., the model that captures the largest proportion of significant channels during speech and/or music perception (Figure 7A), yields for both classes of stimuli a similar TRF shape (Figure 7E) as well as similar prediction accuracy scores (Pearson's r), of up to 0.55 (Figure 7F).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: The peakRate & LF model yields similar prediction accuracy scores (Pearson's r) of up to 0.55 for both speech and music.
source: Finally, the peakRate & LF model, i.e., the model that captures the largest proportion of significant channels during speech and/or music perception (Figure 7A), yields for both classes of stimuli a similar TRF shape (Figure 7E) as well as similar prediction accuracy scores (Pearson's r), of up to 0.55 (Figure 7F).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: During speech or music perception, the auditory cortex is mostly connected to the rest of the brain through slow neural dynamics, with approximately 33% of channels showing coherence values higher than the surrogate distribution at delta rate.
source: Seed-based connectivity analyses first revealed that, during speech or music perception, the auditory cortex is mostly connected to the rest of the brain through slow neural dynamics, with ~33% of the channels showing coherence values higher than the surrogate distribution at delta rate, and only ~12% at HFa (Figure 8, see also Figure 8—figure supplement 1 for uncategorized, continuous results).
evidence: This finding is supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Only approximately 12% of channels show coherence values higher than the surrogate distribution at high-frequency activity during speech or music perception.
source: Seed-based connectivity analyses first revealed that, during speech or music perception, the auditory cortex is mostly connected to the rest of the brain through slow neural dynamics, with ~33% of the channels showing coherence values higher than the surrogate distribution at delta rate, and only ~12% at HFa (Figure 8, see also Figure 8—figure supplement 1 for uncategorized, continuous results).
evidence: This finding is supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Across frequencies, most of the significant connections are shared between speech and music (approximately 70%).
source: Across frequencies, most of the significant connections are shared between the two cognitive domains (~70%), followed by preferred (~15%) and selective connections (~12%).
evidence: This finding is based on connectivity analysis results.

claim: Preferred connections account for approximately 15% of significant connections across frequencies.
source: Across frequencies, most of the significant connections are shared between the two cognitive domains (~70%), followed by preferred (~15%) and selective connections (~12%).
evidence: This finding is based on connectivity analysis results.

claim: Selective connections account for approximately 12% of significant connections across frequencies.
source: Across frequencies, most of the significant connections are shared between the two cognitive domains (~70%), followed by preferred (~15%) and selective connections (~12%).
evidence: This finding is based on connectivity analysis results.

claim: Selectivity in connectivity is homogeneously present in all frequency bands.
source: Selectivity is nonetheless homogeneously present in all frequency bands (Figure 8).
evidence: This observation is based on connectivity analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Selectivity in connectivity is frequency-specific.
source: Importantly, selectivity is again frequency-specific (Figure 9).
evidence: This finding is supported by cross-frequency connectivity analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: The percentage of total connections being selective to speech or music is at zero for all frequency bands except for the delta range.
source: Estimating the cross-frequency channel selectivity, the percentage of total connections being selective to speech or music is at zero for all frequency bands except for the delta range (speech = 0.19%; music = 0.06%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cross-frequency connectivity analysis.

claim: In the delta range, 0.19% of connections are selective to speech and 0.06% are selective to music.
source: Estimating the cross-frequency channel selectivity, the percentage of total connections being selective to speech or music is at zero for all frequency bands except for the delta range (speech = 0.19%; music = 0.06%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cross-frequency connectivity analysis.

claim: Selectivity in connectivity is only visible at the level of frequency-specific distributed networks.
source: Hence, selectivity is only visible at the level of frequency-specific distributed networks.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cross-frequency connectivity analysis.

claim: No anatomical regional selectivity is observed in connectivity analysis.
source: Finally, here again no anatomical regional selectivity is observed, i.e., not a single cortical region is solely selective to speech or music.
evidence: This finding is based on population prevalence analysis of connectivity data shown in Figure 10.

claim: In every cortical region, the majority of patients show shared responses at the regional level in connectivity analysis.
source: Rather, in every cortical region, the majority of patients show shared responses at the regional level, as estimated by the population prevalence analysis (Figure 10).
evidence: This finding is supported by population prevalence analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: Previous work has reported that written or spoken language selectively activates a left-lateralized functional cortical network.
source: Previous work has reported that written or spoken language selectively activates a left-lateralized functional cortical network (Chen et al., 2023; Fedorenko et al., 2011; Fedorenko and Blank, 2020; Malik-Moraleda et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from cited literature.

claim: Strong and selective cortical responses to language were not visible during the presentation of short musical excerpts in previous functional MRI studies.
source: In particular, in previous functional MRI studies, these strong and selective cortical responses were not visible during the presentation of short musical excerpts, and are hypothesized to index linguistic processes (Chen et al., 2023; Fedorenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from cited literature.

claim: In the superior temporal gyrus, specific and separate neural populations for speech, music, and song are visible.
source: Moreover, in the superior temporal gyrus, specific and separate neural populations for speech, music, and song are visible (Boebinger et al., 2021; Norman-Haignere et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from cited literature.

claim: Selective responses in the superior temporal gyrus are independent of both low-level acoustic features and higher-order linguistic meaning.
source: These selective responses, not visible in primary cortical regions, seem independent of both low-level acoustic features and higher-order linguistic meaning (Norman-Haignere et al., 2015), and could subtend intermediate representations (Giordano et al., 2023) such as domain-dependent predictions (McCarty et al., 2023; Sankaran et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from cited literature.

claim: Different communicative signals can exploit distinct acoustic niches to target specific neural networks.
source: Recent studies have shown that some communicative signals (e.g. alarm, emotional, linguistic) can exploit distinct acoustic niches to target specific neural networks and trigger reactions adapted to the intent of the emitter (Albouy et al., 2020; Arnal et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from cited literature.

claim: Different subspaces of spectro-temporal representations encode distinct information types: slow temporal modulations for meaning (speech), fast temporal modulations for alarms (screams), and spectral modulations for melodies.
source: Using neurally relevant spectro-temporal representations (MPS), these studies show that different subspaces encode distinct information types: slow temporal modulations for meaning (speech), fast temporal modulations for alarms (screams), and spectral modulations for melodies (Albouy et al., 2020; Arnal et al., 2015; Arnal et al., 2019; Flinker et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from cited literature.

claim: 10 minutes of instrumental music was enough to activate cortical regions classically labeled as speech or language-selective.
source: In this context, in the current study we did not observe a single anatomical region for which speech selectivity was present, in any of our analyses. In other words, 10 min of instrumental music was enough to activate cortical regions classically labeled as speech (or language)-selective.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: The study reports spatially distributed and frequency-specific patterns of shared, preferred, or selective neural responses and connectivity fingerprints.
source: On the contrary, we report spatially distributed and frequency-specific patterns of shared, preferred, or selective neural responses and connectivity fingerprints.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Domain-selective brain regions should be considered as a set of functionally homogeneous but spatially distributed voxels, instead of anatomical landmarks.
source: This indicates that domain-selective brain regions should be considered as a set of functionally homogeneous but spatially distributed voxels, instead of anatomical landmarks.
evidence: This is an interpretation and conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Alpha/beta rhythms play a role in predicting upcoming stimuli and modulating sensory processing and associated spiking.
source: For instance, alpha/beta rhythms play a role in predicting upcoming stimuli and modulating sensory processing and associated spiking (Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Bastos et al., 2020; Morillon and Baillet, 2017; Saleh et al., 2010; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Slower dynamics in the delta/theta range contribute to speech tracking, segmentation, and decoding.
source: Also slower dynamics in the delta/theta range have been described to play a major role in cognitive processes and in particular for speech perception, contributing to speech tracking, segmentation, and decoding (Ding et al., 2017; Doelling et al., 2014; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Gross et al., 2013; Keitel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activations and deactivations can co-occur in the same spatial location across different frequency bands.
source: Importantly, we here addressed both activations and deactivations that can co-occur in the same spatial location across different frequency bands (Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999; Proix et al., 2022) and indeed observed that the domain selectivity observed within our restricted stimulus set is frequency-specific, meaning that domain selectivity is marginal when considering the entire spectrum of activity of a given sEEG channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and the study's findings.

claim: Domain selectivity is marginal when considering the entire spectrum of activity of a given sEEG channel.
source: Importantly, we here addressed both activations and deactivations that can co-occur in the same spatial location across different frequency bands (Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999; Proix et al., 2022) and indeed observed that the domain selectivity observed within our restricted stimulus set is frequency-specific, meaning that domain selectivity is marginal when considering the entire spectrum of activity of a given sEEG channel.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Ecological auditory stimuli are more prone to elicit distributed and dynamical neural responses than shorter, simpler stimuli.
source: Third, the ecological auditory stimuli we used are longer and more complex than stimuli used in previous studies and hence more prone to elicit distributed and dynamical neural responses (Hasson et al., 2010; Sonkusare et al., 2019; Theunissen et al., 2000) and they require, in the case of music, for instance, more complex representations of melody and rhythm motifs contributing to stronger representations of meter, tonality, and groove (Boebinger et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study's analytical approach does not allow to directly isolate specific brain operations.
source: While listening to natural speech and music rests on cognitively relevant neural processes, our analytical approach, extending over a rather long period of time, does not allow to directly isolate specific brain operations.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study's methodology.

claim: The modeling approach revealed that acoustic dynamics are strongly tracked by auditory neural dynamics.
source: Our modeling approach, although lacking the modeling of melodic and linguistic features, was targeting the temporal dynamics of the speech and music stimuli. Beyond confirming that acoustic dynamics are strongly tracked by auditory neural dynamics, it revealed, investigating the entire cortex, that such neural tracking also occurs well outside of auditory regions—up to motor and inferior frontal areas (Figure 7B; see also Chalas et al., 2022; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013).
evidence: This finding is supported by the TRF analysis and cited literature.

claim: Neural tracking of acoustic dynamics occurs well outside of auditory regions, up to motor and inferior frontal areas.
source: Our modeling approach, although lacking the modeling of melodic and linguistic features, was targeting the temporal dynamics of the speech and music stimuli. Beyond confirming that acoustic dynamics are strongly tracked by auditory neural dynamics, it revealed, investigating the entire cortex, that such neural tracking also occurs well outside of auditory regions—up to motor and inferior frontal areas (Figure 7B; see also Chalas et al., 2022; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013).
evidence: This finding is supported by the TRF analysis shown in Figure 7B and cited literature.

claim: The spatial map of speech dynamics encoding is very similar to former reports of brain regions belonging to the language system.
source: Of note, this spatial map of speech dynamics encoding is very similar to former reports of the brain regions belonging to the language system (Diachek et al., 2020).
evidence: This observation is made by comparing the study's findings to cited literature.

claim: Low-frequency activity clearly better encodes acoustic features than high-frequency amplitude.
source: But, here again, adopting an approach that investigates both low and high frequencies of the neural signal—an approach that is not enough embraced in intracranial EEG studies (Proix et al., 2022)—reveals that the LF activity clearly better encodes acoustic features than the HFa amplitude (Figure 7A).
evidence: This finding is supported by the TRF model comparison shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The results point to a massive amount of shared neural response to speech and music, well beyond the auditory cortex.
source: In conclusion, our results point to a massive amount of shared neural response to speech and music, well beyond the auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: The study shows the interest of considering shared, preferred, and selective responses when investigating domain selectivity.
source: They also show the interest of considering shared, preferred, and selective responses when investigating domain selectivity.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion drawn from the study.

claim: These three classes of responses should be considered in respect to activation or deactivation patterns, different frequency bands, and power spectrum and connectivity approaches.
source: Importantly these three classes of responses should be considered in respect to (1) activation or deactivation patterns compared to a baseline, (2) different frequency bands, and (3) power spectrum (activity) and connectivity approaches.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the study's approach.

claim: The data point to an absence of anatomical regional selectivity for speech and music.
source: While our data point to an absence of anatomical regional selectivity for speech and music, such a selectivity still exists at the level of a spatially distributed and frequency-specific network.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Selectivity for speech and music exists at the level of a spatially distributed and frequency-specific network.
source: While our data point to an absence of anatomical regional selectivity for speech and music, such a selectivity still exists at the level of a spatially distributed and frequency-specific network.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The inconsistency with previous findings may be limited to the idea that some anatomical regions are selective to speech or music processing.
source: Thus, the inconsistency with previous findings may be limited to the idea that some anatomical regions are selective to speech or music processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the study's findings relate to previous literature.

claim: The two points of view can be reconciled when considering a fine-grained network approach allowing selectivity to coexist for speech and music within the same anatomical region.
source: However, the two points of view can be reconciled when considering a fine-grained network approach allowing selectivity to coexist for speech and music within the same anatomical region.
evidence: This is a proposed reconciliation of the study's findings with previous literature.

claim: 18 patients (10 females, mean age 30 years, range 8-54 years) with pharmacoresistant epilepsy participated in the study.
source: 18 patients (10 females, mean age 30 years, range 8–54 years) with pharmacoresistant epilepsy participated in the study.
evidence: This is demographic information about the study participants.

claim: All patients were French native speakers.
source: All patients were French native speakers.
evidence: This is demographic information about the study participants.

claim: Neuropsychological assessments indicated that all patients had intact language functions and met the criteria for normal hearing.
source: Neuropsychological assessments carried out before sEEG recordings indicated that all patients had intact language functions and met the criteria for normal hearing.
evidence: This is information about the clinical characteristics of the study participants.

claim: In none of the patients were the auditory areas part of their epileptogenic zone.
source: In none of them were the auditory areas part of their epileptogenic zone as identified by experienced epileptologists.
evidence: This is information about the clinical characteristics of the study participants.

claim: Patients provided informed consent prior to the experimental session.
source: Patients provided informed consent prior to the experimental session, and the experimental protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the French Institute of Health (IRB00003888).
evidence: This is information about the ethical approval of the study.

claim: The experimental protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the French Institute of Health (IRB00003888).
source: Patients provided informed consent prior to the experimental session, and the experimental protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the French Institute of Health (IRB00003888).
evidence: This is information about the ethical approval of the study.

claim: The cohort consists of 13 unilateral implantations (10 left, 3 right) and 5 bilateral implantations.
source: The cohort consists of 13 unilateral implantations (10 left, 3 right) and 5 bilateral implantations, yielding a total of 271 electrodes and 3371 contacts (see Figure 1C and D for electrodes localization).
evidence: This is information about the electrode implantations in the study participants.

claim: The cohort yielded a total of 271 electrodes and 3371 contacts.
source: The cohort consists of 13 unilateral implantations (10 left, 3 right) and 5 bilateral implantations, yielding a total of 271 electrodes and 3371 contacts (see Figure 1C and D for electrodes localization).
evidence: This is quantitative information about the data collected.

claim: Patients passively listened to approximately 10 minutes of storytelling (577 s, La sorcière de la rue Mouffetard).
source: In the main experimental session, patients passively listened to ~10 min of storytelling (Gripari, 2004); 577 s, La sorcière de la rue Mouffetard (Gripari, 2004) and ~10 min of instrumental music (580 s, Reflejos del Sur, Oneness, 2006) separated by 3 min of rest.
evidence: This is information about the experimental stimuli and procedure.

claim: Patients passively listened to approximately 10 minutes of instrumental music (580 s, Reflejos del Sur, Oneness, 2006).
source: In the main experimental session, patients passively listened to ~10 min of storytelling (Gripari, 2004); 577 s, La sorcière de la rue Mouffetard (Gripari, 2004) and ~10 min of instrumental music (580 s, Reflejos del Sur, Oneness, 2006) separated by 3 min of rest.
evidence: This is information about the experimental stimuli and procedure.

claim: Speech and music stimuli were separated by 3 minutes of rest.
source: In the main experimental session, patients passively listened to ~10 min of storytelling (Gripari, 2004); 577 s, La sorcière de la rue Mouffetard (Gripari, 2004) and ~10 min of instrumental music (580 s, Reflejos del Sur, Oneness, 2006) separated by 3 min of rest.
evidence: This is information about the experimental procedure.

claim: Speech and music excerpts were presented at approximately 75 dBA.
source: Speech and music excerpts were presented at ~75 dBA (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is information about the acoustic properties of the stimuli.

claim: The signal was offline re-referenced using bipolar montage to increase spatial sensitivity and reduce passive volume conduction from neighboring regions.
source: To increase spatial sensitivity and reduce passive volume conduction from neighboring regions (Mercier et al., 2017; Mercier et al., 2022), the signal was offline re-referenced using bipolar montage.
evidence: This is information about the data preprocessing methods.

claim: Bipolar channels located outside of the brain were removed from the data (3%).
source: Based on the brain segmentation performed using SPM12 methods through the FieldTrip toolbox, bipolar channels located outside of the brain were removed from the data (3%).
evidence: This is information about the data preprocessing and quality control.

claim: On average, 18% of channels were tagged as artifacted channels.
source: Channels with a variance greater than 2*IQR (interquartile range, i.e. a non-parametric estimate of the standard deviation)—on either the broadband or high-frequency signals—were tagged as artifacted channels (on average 18% of the channels).
evidence: This is information about the data quality and artifact rejection.
